newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Peseta surges after cen bank releases grip.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Peseta surges after cen bank releases grip.

text.p: The peseta stormed through the 84.00 per mark level on Friday after the Bank of Spain released its tight grip on the currency and refrained from intervening, traders said.

After months of champing at the bit, the peseta broke free to trade at levels not seen since last May around 83.55 per mark, stabilising by midday at around 83.65, compared with late Thursday levels of 84.09.
But some analysts said they did not believe the peseta had seen the last of the Bank of Spain's hand with the central bank just biding time before the next onslaught of intervention.
"The central bank is probably just sitting back to see what happens which is normal after heavy intervention," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
"It's clear though that they haven't been as successful this time as in the past as there is more strength behind the flows this time," he added.

Traders said the Bank of Spain was thought to have been intervening heavily since Wednesday to brake the peseta's appreciation, selling pesetas against the mark. The central bank does not comment on its intervention policy.

In recent months, the peseta has remained at the mercy of the central bank which is thought to be keen to hold the currency in the 84.00 to 85.00 per mark band in the run up to a single European currency.

However considerable inflows into Spain's bond and equity markets, sparked partly by the belief that Spain will be in the first wave to join Europe's monetary union (EMU), have exerted signficant pressure on the peseta to appreciate.
Analysts said a feeble performance from the mark on Friday had given the Spanish currency a further boost.

"The peseta's rise is a result at the moment of a general weakness in the market, but the Bank of Spain will probably still want to hold the currency close to 84.00 per mark," said Maria Victoria Nunez, an analyst at Societe Generale in Madrid.
Some analysts said disapproving looks from EU partners who may prefer a stronger peseta and billowing currency reserves may be taking their toll on the central bank.
Other said the break in intervention may be a sign that the Bank of Spain had decided to turn to other methods to control the currency.
"It is possible that the Bank of Spain may resort to other instruments and (for example) lower repo rates, perhaps at the next auction," said Carmen Hernansanz, an analyst at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
This would, however, depend on how the peseta behaved in coming sessions, she added.
A stabilising of the currency to around 83.66 per mark by 1210 GMT illustrated that there were still fears of Bank of Spain intervention, some traders said.
They warned that the peseta could also become a victim of profit taking later in the session dragging it back toward 84.00 per mark.
